job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Tomas Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight, have toast with my sister Mika before she leaves for school, and then I sit at the desk in my old bedroom with the job boards open. I've sent 58 applications since June for audit and accounts jobs. Afternoons I walk to the library on Station Road because the house gets loud, and I check my email about every twenty minutes, which I know is silly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your degree, and what did you do on your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Accounting and finance, at the city university, a good result but not a first. I did eight weeks at a small audit firm, Marsh and Dole, checking supplier invoices against bank records with a ruler and a highlighter, honestly. I liked it, and nobody there ever mentioned an AI tool, which suited me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, finally somebody admits the hype was a sales pitch. At home I'd tell my dad that the big firms oversold it to their shareholders and now we can all go back to normal. Online I'd probably stay quiet, because I don't trust anything posted about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes and I still have to get through 58 applications and counting. The routine checking I did at Marsh and Dole, matching invoices, is exactly what these tools claim to do, so even a small saving could mean one fewer junior hire. That's what worries me when I'm alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, ten a week, mostly to mid-size firms near home, and I'd go to the careers evening at the university again. I'd also join the graduate branch of the accountants' union, which my dad says is worth the fee. I wouldn't touch any AI tool, even if the job ad asks for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels flat, like waiting at a bus stop where the buses are late but still running. I'm not frightened, just tired of explaining to relatives why I'm still at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never touch an AI tool, but a job ad might ask for it. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd never touch an AI tool, but a job ad might ask for it. What then?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame most for how hard the job search feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a problem, and I know that. I'd probably take a short course through the union rather than teach myself, because I like learning in a room with people. I just don't want to be the person typing questions into a chatbot all day.

say: I'd say the **hype** was a sales pitch for shareholders and we can go back to normal.
I'd tell my dad the big firms oversold it, and I'd stay quiet online.
think: I still face **58 applications** and counting, and routine checking could shrink junior hiring anyway.
Even a small saving from software could mean one fewer graduate hire at the firms I want.
do: Send **ten applications a week**, mostly to mid-size firms near home.
Join the graduate branch of the accountants' **union** and go to the university careers evening.
Refuse AI tools, even if an advert asks for them.
feel: Flat and **tired**, like waiting for a late bus, with no real fear yet.
S0.quote: I'm not frightened, just tired of explaining to relatives why I'm still at home.
fieldNote: Resistant to technology by habit, so he avoids the one skill adverts now mention.
Leans on **union membership** as his plan, which fits his progressive views.
Family cushion keeps him steady but the open-ended job search wears on him.

steps.text: Send ten applications a week to mid-size firms near home
Join the graduate branch of the accountants' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where employers use the word efficiency to mean fewer graduates. At the union evening I'd argue for rules on how many junior roles a firm can swap for software. To friends I'd say it's not a revolution, it's a slow squeeze on people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the checking and matching work that juniors learn on is the first thing that goes. That was my whole internship at Marsh and Dole. If the bottom rung is software, I don't know how you ever become a senior accountant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to the public sector and housing associations, where there are rules and unions. I'd also finally pay for a six-week short course on audit technology, because I can't avoid it forever. I'd keep living at home through the first year and keep my savings untouched rather than spend them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick, to be honest. The ladder is still there, but the first four rungs are missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the short course be a change of heart about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would the short course be a change of heart about AI?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which job would you rather have, a private firm or the public sector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one. I'd do it because the course sits in a classroom, with a teacher and other graduates, not because I've warmed to it. If it helps me get through one interview, it's worth the fee.

say: I'd say **efficiency** often just means fewer graduates, and rules should limit swapping junior jobs for software.
I'd tell friends it's a slow **squeeze** on people like me.
think: The matching and checking work juniors learn on goes first, so the **bottom rung** may vanish.
I worry how anyone becomes a senior accountant without that start.
do: Widen the search to **public sector** bodies and housing associations.
Pay for a six-week audit technology **short course** in a classroom.
Stay at home and keep the savings untouched.
feel: A bit **sick**, like the first rungs of the ladder are missing.
S1.quote: The ladder is still there, but the first four rungs are missing.
fieldNote: Sees the threat clearly through his own internship, which was pure checking work.
Willing to learn only in a **classroom** with people, a sign of his resistance.

steps.text: Apply to housing associations and public bodies as well as audit firms
Pay for a six-week audit technology course in a classroom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless, and governments should have a plan before it happens. Two years is nothing. I'd sign anything that makes firms prove they have a plan for the staff they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree is worth very little by 2028. If AI can do any thinking work cheaper, who hires a graduate with eight weeks of invoice checking behind him? I'd be competing with software that never sleeps, and I can't even say I know how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for anything with a human in the middle, like a bank branch or a hospital finance office, and ask my dad about his depot. I'd also go to the union and push for a public jobs scheme. And I'd stop pretending I can ignore the tools and finally spend a month learning them, even though I hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and angry at the same time. I lie awake doing sums on how long my savings last without a wage, which is maybe a year and a half if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Mika about her own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Mika about her future?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop ignoring the tools. What changed your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister Mika to learn something with her hands and a person across the table, like nursing or plumbing. That's not what I'd have said a year ago, and it feels strange saying it with a degree behind me.

say: I'd call it **reckless**: two years is nothing, so firms must prove they have a plan for replaced staff.
I'd back a **public jobs scheme** through the union.
think: My degree could be worth little by **2028**, and I'd compete with software that never sleeps.
I'm ashamed I can't even claim to know the tools.
do: Apply for roles with a **person in the middle**, such as bank branches and hospital finance offices.
Spend a month **learning AI tools**, which I hate doing.
Push the union for a public jobs scheme.
feel: **Scared** and angry together, doing sums on how long savings last.
S2.quote: I'd tell my sister Mika to learn something with her hands and a person across the table, like nursing or plumbing.
fieldNote: His resistance cracks here and he reluctantly accepts he must learn the tools.
Savings give him **eighteen months**, which he counts nightly.
Advises his younger sister away from desk work, an honest reversal.

steps.text: Apply for bank branch and hospital finance office jobs with people contact
Spend one month learning basic AI tools for audit work
Sign union petitions for a public jobs scheme
Advise Mika to study nursing instead of office work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that nobody can claim they weren't warned. At work I'd urge firms to start training graduates in how to supervise software. To friends I'd say get involved in your union now, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I get a window. If I land a job in the next year, I'd have four years to become the person who checks what the software produces, which is more than a graduate has in the two-year version. But I might still be let go in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent offer, even in a firm I don't love, then study for my chartered exams in the evenings. I'd save a third of every pay cheque. I'd also learn the audit software at work, slowly, because I'd have a boss to show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the fast one, but still a weight. Five years feels long when you're 23 and short when you think about a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take the first decent offer. Is that different from how you search now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd take the first decent offer. Is that different from how you search now?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'm picky right now because I can afford to be. My family would carry me for a while, and I've been using that as an excuse. With five years on the clock, I'd stop being fussy and start the clock on my career.

say: I'd say five years means **nobody can claim** they weren't warned, so unions should get involved now.
I'd urge firms to train graduates to supervise software.
think: I get a **window**: land a job within a year and I'd have four years to become the checker.
I might still be let go at the end.

S3.quote: Five years feels long when you're 23 and short when you think about a mortgage.

Time pressure finally makes him choose a plan, which he says plainly.

steps.text: Accept the first decent graduate offer within the next year

Put a third of every pay cheque into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to rebuild how work is shared. Shorter weeks, retraining paid by firms, proper public support. I'd tell friends it's a long runway, so use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine if I get started now. In ten years I could be a manager who understands both the numbers and the software. The danger is that I stay at home applying to the same firms and let the years slip by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job within the year, get my chartered exams done by 27, and learn the tools on the job. I'd also stay in the union and maybe become a rep, like my dad. I'd keep a savings habit and maybe think about buying a small flat around 28.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. Ten years is a decent amount of time, and I can picture a life in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside to having ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is there a downside to having ten years?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why become a union rep like your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it makes me lazy. If nothing is urgent, I put things off, and that's how I've spent the last few months. A deadline is actually better for me, which is a funny thing to say.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway**: shorter weeks, firm-funded retraining and public support can be built.
I'd tell friends to use the time.
think: If I start now, I could become a manager who understands both **numbers and software**.
My real danger is drifting at home for years.
do: Take a job within the year and finish **chartered exams** by 27.
Learn the tools on the job and become a **union rep** like my dad.
Keep saving, maybe for a small flat near 28.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, with a worry that a long runway makes me lazy.
S4.quote: If nothing is urgent, I put things off, and that's how I've spent the last few months.
fieldNote: Admits slack **deadlines** suit him badly, a self-aware point.
Imagines a whole career path, the first time he does in the interview.
Anchors his hopes in union life.

steps.text: Start a graduate job within the year and finish chartered exams by 27

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, no question, because two years leaves no room to learn what I resisted. What would help is a guaranteed route for graduates, such as paid traineeships, and employers who must say how many junior posts they cut. I'd also like someone to teach me the tools without making me feel stupid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as against technology as I sound. I'm against being told to adapt alone. If someone sat with me in a room and showed me, I'd learn.

headlineQuote: I'm against being told to adapt alone. If someone sat with me in a room and showed me, I'd learn.
portrait: Tomas is 23, an accounting graduate living with his parents and sister Mika, with **58 applications** and no offer.
He has savings, no debt and a family cushion, but his habit of avoiding new technology leaves him exposed.
His progressive views make him blame **employers and shareholders**, and he turns to unions and public schemes.
In the fast scenarios he reverses his stance, accepting he must learn the tools, and advises his sister away from desk work.
Longer timelines make him hopeful but also lazy, so he says a **deadline** would help him.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries him most, because it leaves no time to learn what he has avoided.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **traineeships** for graduates and employers made to report how many junior posts they cut.
Classroom teaching of AI tools that doesn't make him feel stupid.
